q.q: What is malware?
o: Any software that has not been patched against known security vulnerabilities
Any program that floods a server with traffic so genuine users cannot reach it
Any software written to damage or disrupt a system or to gain unauthorised access to it
Any message that manipulates a person into revealing a password or other details
q.why: Malware is malicious software written to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access. Flooding a server is DoS and manipulating people is social engineering.

q.q: Which type of malware spreads across a network on its own, without any user action?
o: Virus
Worm
Trojan
Spyware
q.why: A worm is standalone and self-replicating. A virus needs a host file and user action; a Trojan does not replicate.

q.q: A program pretends to be a free game. Once installed it opens a back door giving an attacker remote control. What is it?
o: Worm
Virus
Trojan
Ransomware
q.why: A Trojan is disguised as legitimate software that the user installs willingly and does not replicate.

q.q: Which feature distinguishes a virus from a worm?
o: A virus spreads itself across a network without help
A virus needs a host file and user action to spread
A virus is disguised as software the user wants
A virus always encrypts files and demands payment
q.why: A virus attaches to a host and spreads when the host is run or shared; a worm is standalone and spreads itself.

q.q: A keylogger secretly captures a user's passwords and sends them to an attacker. Which type of malware is this?
o: Spyware
Trojan
Ransomware
Worm
q.why: Spyware secretly records activity, such as a keylogger capturing passwords, and sends it to the attacker. It may be installed by a Trojan, but the keylogger itself is spyware.

q.q: What does ransomware do?
o: Copies itself across the network through unpatched systems
Secretly records keystrokes and sends them to the attacker
Encrypts files and demands payment for the key
Attaches itself to a host file and deletes data
q.why: Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment, often in cryptocurrency, for the decryption key.

q.q: How did the 2017 WannaCry attack spread through NHS organisations?
o: As a virus attached to files shared by staff on USB sticks
As a Trojan disguised as an NHS software update
As a worm through an unpatched Windows vulnerability
As spyware bundled with a free web browser plug-in
q.why: WannaCry spread as a worm through an unpatched Windows vulnerability and then encrypted files.

q.q: What is the best defence against losing data to ransomware?
o: Paying the ransom quickly before the price rises
Recent backups held on the same network drive
Deleting the ransom note and restarting the server
Recent backups held separately from the network
q.why: Separate backups let files be restored without paying. Backups on the same network may be encrypted too, and paying gives no guarantee.

q.q: Which statement about Trojans is correct?
o: They replicate across a network without any user action
They do not replicate; the user installs them willingly
They attach to a host file and spread when it is shared
They encrypt the user's files and then demand a payment
q.why: Trojans do not replicate; the user installs them willingly. Viruses and worms both copy themselves.

q.q: Malware infects a whole office network within hours, with nobody opening any file. Why does this point to a worm rather than a virus?
o: Viruses spread very fast by themselves; worms depend on users sharing files
Worms are disguised as useful software, so staff install them without noticing
Viruses only infect one computer and can never spread across a network at all
Worms spread very fast by themselves; viruses depend on users sharing files
q.why: A worm needs no host or user action and can infect a whole network in hours; a virus spreads more slowly as users share files.

q.q: Which law makes unauthorised access to computer material an offence in the UK?
o: Data Protection Act 2018
Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988
Computer Misuse Act 1990
Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000
q.why: The Computer Misuse Act 1990 (as amended) makes simply accessing material without permission an offence.

q.q: A hacker uses software that tries every possible combination of characters to find a password. What is this called?
o: A dictionary attack
SQL injection
Pretexting
A brute-force attack
q.why: Brute force tries every combination; a dictionary attack tries likely words from a list.

q.q: A web form does not validate its input, so database commands typed into it are run by the server. What is this attack?
o: Brute-force attack
Spear phishing
Denial of service
SQL injection
q.why: SQL injection exploits forms that do not validate input, letting typed database commands be run by the server.

q.q: What does social engineering target?
o: Unpatched servers
People
Network cables
Backup tapes
q.why: Social engineering attacks the person rather than the technology, exploiting trust, urgency and fear.

q.q: An email addressed to a finance officer by name mentions her manager and a recent project, asking her to log in to a link. What is this?
o: Pretexting
Smishing
Spear phishing
Vishing
q.why: Spear phishing is a phishing message tailored to one person using details such as name, job and manager.

q.q: A visitor at reception claims to be from the IT support company and asks a member of staff for her password to 'fix an account problem'. Which attack is this best described as?
o: Smishing
Pretexting
Spear phishing
Brute force
q.why: Pretexting means inventing a believable story, such as posing as IT support, to obtain a password.

q.q: Phishing carried out by text message is called...
o: vishing
pretexting
smishing
spear phishing
q.why: Smishing uses SMS text messages; vishing uses phone calls.

q.q: What is the main countermeasure to phishing, according to the notes?
o: A hardware firewall at the boundary of the network
Full backups taken weekly and stored off-site
Staff awareness training, with email filtering and MFA
Encryption of all laptops and USB sticks
q.why: Phishing is countered mainly by staff awareness training, together with email filtering and multi-factor authentication.

q.q: What is the main effect of a DDoS attack on an online shop?
o: Customer card details are stolen from the database
The shop's files are encrypted for a ransom
The web server's hardware is physically damaged
Genuine customers cannot reach the website
q.why: A DDoS floods the server so genuine users cannot reach it; the main harm is lost availability, not stolen data.

q.q: Why is a distributed denial of service attack harder to filter than a simple denial of service attack?
o: Traffic comes from thousands of compromised devices in a botnet
The attack uses SQL injection to bypass the firewall rules
The traffic is encrypted, so the firewall cannot read it
The attacker uses stolen passwords to log in as real users
q.why: A DDoS uses a botnet, so traffic comes from many addresses and is much harder to block.

q.q: What is an insider threat?
o: A threat from hackers who gain unauthorised access from outside the network
A threat from employees or contractors who misuse access they legitimately hold
A threat from malware that is installed inside the network by a Trojan
A threat from hardware failure on a server held inside the building
q.why: An insider threat comes from people inside the organisation misusing legitimate access.

q.q: Why is a malicious insider hard to detect?
o: They always use worms, which hide themselves from anti-malware software
They use access they legitimately hold, so the activity looks like normal work
They only attack from outside the network, so audit logs do not record them
They never change any data, so there is nothing for anyone to notice
q.why: Because their access is legitimate, their activity is harder to spot.

q.q: An employee leaves an unencrypted laptop on a train. What kind of threat is this?
o: A careless insider
A malicious insider
Social engineering
Hardware failure
q.why: Careless insiders cause breaches through mistakes like losing an unencrypted laptop or emailing the wrong person. The notes say they cause even more breaches than malicious insiders.

q.q: A power surge corrupts a database part-way through an update. Which category of threat is this?
o: A deliberate threat: denial of service
An accidental threat: power problems
An insider threat: a careless employee
An accidental threat: human error
q.why: Power cuts or surges are accidental threats listed under power problems.

q.q: Which is an accidental threat to data?
o: A phishing email sent to the finance department
Ransomware arriving through an email attachment
A DDoS attack on the company's booking website
A disk crash on a server that has no redundancy
q.why: Hardware failure is accidental; the other options are deliberate attacks.

q.q: Within how many hours must a qualifying personal data breach normally be reported to the Information Commission under the UK GDPR?
q.why: A breach that risks harm to individuals must normally be reported within 72 hours of the organisation becoming aware of it.

q.q: A dental clinic's server fails and staff cannot see the appointment list for a day. Which answer best applies the consequence of downtime to this scenario?
o: The clinic loses money because computers are expensive
Patients are turned away, so the clinic loses income and goodwill
The clinic must report the failure to the police within 72 hours
The clinic's data is now archived and must be indexed
q.why: Consequences should be applied to the scenario: patients turned away means lost income and trust. Generic statements score less.

q.q: Which consequence of a breach of customers' personal data could involve fines?
o: Loss of the company's backup window
A shorter recovery time objective
Reduced network bandwidth
Regulatory action under the UK GDPR
q.why: A reportable breach may lead to regulatory action and fines by the Information Commission.

q.q: What is data archiving?
o: Moving inactive data to separate, secure, long-term storage
Copying current data to separate storage each night
Deleting inactive data once it is no longer used
Encrypting active data before it is transmitted
q.why: Archiving moves inactive data out of the live system, keeping it retrievable. Copying current data is backup.

q.q: At a further education college, which is inactive data?
o: Current students' timetables
Current students' attendance records
Records of students who left five years ago
Fees owed by current students
q.why: Inactive data is rarely used but must be kept; the other options are needed day to day (active data).

q.q: Why is an archive indexed?
o: So that records can be located and retrieved later
So that the archived data is encrypted at rest
So that the archive becomes active data again
So that the archive is backed up automatically
q.why: An index means a record can be found again quickly when needed.

q.q: A loyalty-card system holds two million customers but only 300,000 are active. What is the main benefit of archiving the inactive ones?
o: The inactive customers' data no longer needs protecting under the law
The archived records become instantly available whenever needed
Day-to-day processing, reports and backups become much faster
The live system no longer needs any backups to be taken
q.why: The main reason to archive is performance: the live system works through fewer records.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of archiving?
o: The live system becomes slower to search
Older data can no longer be kept for audit
Backups of the live system take longer
Archived data is not immediately available
q.why: Archived data is not immediately available and must be searched for; the live system and backups actually get faster.

q.q: Why can archived data be kept on cheaper storage?
o: It no longer needs to be indexed for retrieval
It is rarely needed, so slower access is acceptable
It is legally exempt from data protection rules
It is compressed so it takes up no extra space
q.why: Archived data can go on cheaper, slower storage because it is rarely accessed; the trade-off is poor access speed.

q.q: Archived records contain customers' personal data. What does the law require?
o: It is still covered by the UK GDPR and should be deleted after a retention period
It is no longer covered by the UK GDPR once it leaves the live system
It must be kept forever in case the customers return to the business
It must be moved back to the live system every year to be checked
q.why: Archived personal data is still covered by the UK GDPR and DPA 2018 and should be kept only for a defined retention period.

q.q: Which statement about archiving and backing up is correct?
o: Archiving copies current data; backing up moves inactive data
Both move data out of the live system to long-term storage
Archiving moves inactive data; backing up copies current data
Both copy current data so the live system can be restored
q.why: Use the key words: archive = move (inactive data); backup = copy (current data).

q.q: After data has been archived, where is it held?
o: Only in the archive
In the live system and the archive
Only in the latest backup
Nowhere, as it has been deleted
q.why: Archiving moves the data out of the live system, so it is held only in the archive.

q.q: Why is backing up a higher priority than archiving?
o: Backups are cheaper to store than archived data
Losing current data has an immediate effect on the organisation
Archived data is illegal to keep for long periods
Backups are taken only at the end of each year
q.why: Current data supports daily operations, so its loss is felt at once; archived data is not needed immediately.

q.q: How often is data typically archived?
o: Regularly and frequently, e.g. nightly or hourly
Occasionally, e.g. at the end of a school or financial year
Every time a transaction is made on the live system
Only when the live system has failed completely
q.why: Archiving is occasional; backups are regular, frequent and usually automated.

q.q: When is data typically retrieved from a backup?
o: When an old record is needed for reference
When an auditor asks for last decade's accounts
When the live system needs to run faster
When the live system fails or data is lost
q.why: Backups are retrieved for recovery after loss; archives are retrieved when an old record is needed for reference.

q.q: A school copies all current pupil data to an external server every night. What is this?
o: A backup
An archive
A restore point
A transaction log
q.why: Copying current data at regular intervals, with the original staying live, is a backup.

q.q: At the end of the year a school moves the records of pupils who have left onto a separate storage system. What is this?
o: Backing up
Data recovery
Archiving
Disaster recovery
q.why: Moving inactive data out of the live system to long-term storage is archiving.

q.q: Why should an organisation also protect its archive by keeping copies?
o: An archive held in only one place could be lost too
Archived data must be restored to the live system each night
The archive replaces the need for backups of live data
Copies make archived data immediately available to staff
q.why: Archives should be protected because an archive held in only one place could also be lost.

q.q: What is a restore point?
o: The physical location where the organisation's backups are stored off-site
A record of exactly what the system looked like at the moment it was backed up
A list of the users who are allowed to restore files from the backups
The time at which a disaster or data loss happened on the system
q.why: A restore point records the system's state at the moment of the backup, so it can be returned precisely to that state.

q.q: What is data recovery?
o: Moving inactive data to separate long-term storage
Copying current data to separate storage at intervals
Recording every change made to a database in order
Using backed-up data to return a system to an earlier correct state
q.why: Data recovery uses backups to return a system to an earlier correct state after loss.

q.q: After restoring the most recent backup, how can changes made since that backup be recovered?
o: By re-applying transactions from a transaction log in order
By restoring the archive over the top of the backup
They cannot be recovered in any way once lost
By creating a new restore point straight away
q.why: Many databases keep a transaction log; re-applying the logged transactions in order rolls the data forward to just before the failure.

q.q: A company backs up nightly. Its server fails at 4pm. How much work is at risk if there is no transaction log?
o: Up to a day's changes since the last backup
Only changes made in the last hour
Nothing, because the backup is complete
All data since the last full archive
q.why: The gap between backups decides how much work is at risk; a nightly backup means up to a day's changes could be lost.

q.q: Why would an airline back up its booking system far more often than a school's coursework server?
o: Airlines are required to archive bookings every hour
Frequent backups make the booking system run faster
Losing even an hour of bookings would be costly and damaging
School data does not need to be backed up at all
q.why: Critical systems back up much more often, or copy changes to a second system, because the data at risk is so valuable.

q.q: Why should backups be stored separately from the original data?
o: Separate storage makes backups faster to create
The law forbids backups on the same premises
A backup in the same place can be destroyed or encrypted with it
Backups in the same place cannot be restored
q.why: A backup kept with the original can be lost in the same fire, theft or ransomware attack.

q.q: Why should an organisation test restoring from its backups?
o: Testing makes each backup smaller to store
Testing replaces the need for a transaction log
Testing means backups need not be automated
A backup that cannot be restored is worthless
q.why: Testing restores proves that the backups actually work.

q.q: Why are backups normally automated?
o: Automated backups do not need any storage space
Automated backups cannot be affected by ransomware
Automated backups never need to be tested
People forget, but automated backups happen reliably on schedule
q.why: Automation ensures backups happen reliably on schedule.

q.q: What is a security policy?
o: A piece of software that scans files for malware and removes it automatically
A set of firewall rules listing permitted IP addresses, ports and protocols
A formal document of rules, procedures and responsibilities for protecting systems and data
An insurance policy that pays for hardware damaged in a fire or flood
q.why: A security policy is the procedural layer of security: formal rules, procedures and responsibilities.

q.q: Organisations protect data with procedural, technical and physical measures. Which layer is a security policy?
o: Technical
Physical
Logical
Procedural
q.why: The security policy is the procedural foundation; firewalls are technical and locks are physical.

q.q: Which section of a security policy would set out the procedure for removing access when someone leaves?
o: Acceptable use
Access control
Incident reporting
Remote working
q.why: Access control covers who may access which data and the procedure for granting and removing access.

q.q: A member of staff receives a suspicious email. Which section of the security policy tells her what to do and how quickly?
o: Acceptable use
Backup and recovery
Incident reporting
Disciplinary consequences
q.why: Incident reporting covers how to report a lost device, phishing email or suspected breach, and how quickly.

q.q: Rules on using VPNs and avoiding public Wi-Fi would appear in which section of a security policy?
o: Remote working
Access control
Devices and removable media
Acceptable use
q.why: Remote working covers VPNs, working in public places and home Wi-Fi.

q.q: Why must a security policy be reviewed regularly?
o: The law requires the policy to be rewritten daily
Threats and technology change over time
Staff must sign a new policy every week
Older policies cannot be enforced by law
q.why: New threats, devices and ways of working need new rules.

q.q: Which three things must happen for a security policy to work?
o: It must be encrypted, archived and backed up
It must be communicated, archived and printed
It must be written, encrypted and filed away
It must be communicated, enforced and reviewed
q.why: Staff must read and sign it, breaches must have consequences backed by technical settings, and it must be reviewed regularly.

q.q: Which combination is genuine multi-factor authentication?
o: A password and a PIN
Two different passwords
A username and a password
A password and a fingerprint
q.why: MFA needs different factor types: something you know plus something you are. A password and PIN are both 'know'.

q.q: A security key or a mobile phone used to log in is which authentication factor?
o: Something you know
Something you are
Something you do
Something you have
q.why: Factors are know (password/PIN), have (phone/security key) and are (fingerprint/face).

q.q: Why does MFA protect an account even if a user's password has been phished?
o: The password is encrypted, so the attacker cannot read the phished copy
The attacker still needs a second, different factor such as the user's phone
The firewall blocks any login attempt from an unknown IP address
The account is locked as soon as the password is typed on a fake page
q.why: MFA combines at least two different factor types, so a stolen password alone is not enough.

q.q: What is the principle of least privilege?
o: Each user gets read-only access to every file
Only managers may log in to the network
Each user must use the shortest password allowed
Each user gets only the access their job needs
q.why: Least privilege limits damage from mistakes, malicious insiders or compromised accounts.

q.q: What does encryption achieve if a laptop holding customer data is stolen?
o: The data cannot be read without the key
The theft of the laptop is prevented
The data is deleted automatically
The laptop cannot be switched on
q.why: Encryption does not stop data being stolen or deleted; it stops stolen data being read.

q.q: Which is a feature of symmetric encryption?
o: A public key encrypts and a private key decrypts, so no secret is shared
It is slower than asymmetric encryption, so it is used only for key exchange
It is computationally expensive, so it is unsuitable for encrypting a disk
The same key encrypts and decrypts, and the main problem is sharing it safely
q.why: Symmetric uses one key, is fast and suits bulk data; its problem is sharing the key. The other options describe asymmetric encryption.

q.q: In asymmetric encryption, which key is used to decrypt a message?
o: The recipient's public key
The shared session key
The recipient's private key
The sender's public key
q.why: In a key pair the public key encrypts and the private key decrypts.

q.q: When a browser connects using HTTPS, how are the two kinds of encryption used together?
o: Symmetric encryption agrees an asymmetric key pair, which encrypts the rest of the traffic
Asymmetric encryption is used for all of the traffic, because it is the faster method
Symmetric encryption is used for the login only, and the rest is sent as plaintext
Asymmetric encryption agrees a symmetric session key, which encrypts the rest of the traffic
q.why: Asymmetric is slower but solves key sharing, so it sets up the connection; the faster symmetric session key encrypts the bulk data.

q.q: What does a firewall do?
o: Examines network traffic against a set of rules and blocks what does not match
Encrypts all files on a device so that stolen data cannot be read by anyone
Records who accessed which files so that misuse by insiders can be detected
Copies current data to separate storage so it can be restored after a loss
q.why: A firewall filters incoming and outgoing traffic by rules such as IP addresses, ports and protocols.

q.q: Which measure mainly counters the threat of lost or stolen laptops and USB sticks?
o: Encryption at rest
A hardware firewall
Least-privilege access rights
Audit logs
q.why: Encryption at rest makes data on lost devices unreadable. Firewalls counter unauthorised network connections.

q.q: An incremental backup copies files changed since...
o: the most recent backup of any kind
the most recent full backup only
the system was first installed
the most recent archive was made
q.why: Incremental = since the last backup of any type (full or incremental). Differential = since the last full backup.

q.q: A differential backup copies files changed since...
o: the most recent backup of any kind
the most recent full backup
the most recent differential backup
the start of the current day
q.why: A differential copies everything changed since the last full backup, so it grows each day.

q.q: Which backup method uses the least storage?
o: Differential
Full
Archive
Incremental
q.why: Each incremental holds only the changes since the previous backup.

q.q: What is the main advantage of a full backup?
o: It is the fastest kind of backup to create
It uses the least storage of all methods
The whole system can be restored from a single backup
It only copies files that have changed
q.why: A full backup gives the simplest restore. It is the slowest and largest to create.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of differential backups?
o: Every previous differential is needed to restore
Each one grows larger until the next full backup
They cannot be used to restore the system
They copy every file whether changed or not
q.why: Changes accumulate since the last full backup, so each differential is bigger than the last.

q.q: Which is the main risk of relying on incremental backups?
o: If the latest differential is corrupt, every change since the full is lost
If any incremental in the chain is corrupt, later changes may be lost
Each incremental grows larger every day until the storage runs out
The whole system must be copied every night, using the most storage
q.why: Restoring needs the full backup plus every incremental in order, so one bad link can lose later changes.

q.q: Why is a full backup every night often wasteful?
o: Full backups cannot be restored without the incrementals taken since the previous one
Only a small fraction of data changes each day, so most copying repeats yesterday's work
Full backups only copy the files that have changed since the previous full backup
Full backups must be stored with the original data, so they are easily destroyed
q.why: Full backups copy everything, changed or not, so most of the work is repeated.

q.q: A firm takes a full backup on Sunday. On Monday files A and B change; on Tuesday only file C changes. What does Tuesday's differential contain?
o: Files A, B and C
File C only
Files A and B only
Every file on the system
q.why: A differential holds every file changed since the last full backup, so it contains A, B and C.

q.q: A firm takes a full backup on Sunday. On Monday files A and B change; on Tuesday only file C changes. What does Tuesday's incremental contain?
o: File C only
Files A, B and C
Files A and B only
Every file on the system
q.why: An incremental holds only files changed since the last backup of any kind (Monday's), so just C.

q.q: A hospital system must be running again as quickly as possible after a failure. Which methods do the notes say this favours?
o: Full or differential backups, because restores are faster
Incremental backups, because they are fastest to create
Incremental backups, because they use the least storage
Archiving, because inactive data is removed from the system
q.why: Where downtime is unacceptable, faster restores matter more than faster backups, favouring full or differential.

q.q: A system uses differential backups. Which backups are needed to restore it?
o: Only the latest differential backup
The last full backup and every differential since
Only the last full backup
The last full backup and the latest differential
q.why: The latest differential holds all changes since the last full backup, so two backups are needed.

q.q: A system uses incremental backups. What is the restore procedure?
o: Restore the last full backup, then only the most recent incremental
Restore every incremental since the full backup, newest first, then the full
Restore the last full backup, then every incremental since, in date order
Restore the most recent incremental only, as it holds every change
q.why: Each incremental must be applied in order after the full backup.

q.q: Why must incremental backups be applied in date order?
o: So that the full backup is no longer needed
So that the latest version of each file ends up in place
So that less storage is used during the restore
So that the transaction log can be deleted
q.why: A file changed several times appears in several incrementals; applying them in order leaves the newest version.

q.q: A firm takes a full backup on Friday night and incrementals every night after. The server fails on Wednesday morning. How many backups must be restored?
q.why: Friday's full plus incrementals from Saturday, Sunday, Monday and Tuesday nights: 1 + 4 = 5.

q.q: A firm takes a full backup on Friday night and differentials every night after. The server fails on Wednesday morning. Which backups are restored?
o: Friday's full backup and every differential since
Tuesday night's differential backup on its own
Friday's full backup and Tuesday night's differential
Friday's full backup and Saturday's differential
q.why: Tuesday's differential contains every change since Friday's full backup.

q.q: After all the backups have been restored, what state is the system in?
o: The state at the last restore point, the time of the most recent backup used
The state just before the failure, with no work lost at all
The state at the time of the last full backup only
The state at the time the system was first installed
q.why: The system is at the last restore point; work after that is lost unless captured in a transaction log.

q.q: How many backups are needed to restore a system that uses only full backups?
q.why: Replace the existing files with the most recent full backup: one backup.

q.q: Why should an organisation practise restores regularly?
o: It reduces the storage that the backups need
Staff learn the procedure and the backups are proven to work
It removes the need to keep a transaction log
It turns incremental backups into full backups
q.why: Practising restores keeps downtime low and proves the backups can be used.

q.q: What is the purpose of a disaster recovery plan?
o: To prevent all disasters from affecting the organisation
To replace the need for regular backups of current data
To move inactive data to secure long-term storage
To minimise the effects of a disaster and resume operations quickly
q.why: Disasters cannot be prevented; the plan is about recovering with the least disruption to customers.

q.q: Which is an example of a deliberate disaster?
o: A major cyber attack
A flood
A fire caused by faulty wiring
Storm damage
q.why: Deliberate disasters include cyber attacks, espionage and terrorism. Fire from wiring is accidental.

q.q: A company kept its backups in the same building as its servers. A fire destroyed the building. Why was recovery impossible?
o: The backups were incremental, so could not be restored
The backups were encrypted and the key was lost
The backups were destroyed along with the originals
The backups were too large to restore in time
q.why: Backups must be stored where the same disaster cannot reach them, i.e. off-site.

q.q: When should a disaster recovery plan be drawn up?
o: As soon as a computerised system is set up
Immediately after the first disaster occurs
When the system is due to be replaced
Only after a simulated test has failed
q.why: The plan should be created when the system is set up and kept up to date as systems change.

q.q: Why must resources such as off-site backups or a standby site be arranged in advance?
o: They cannot be arranged after a disaster has happened
They are cheaper to buy once a disaster has happened
The law forbids buying them during a disaster
They are only needed for simulated tests
q.why: The plan forces the organisation to put resources in place beforehand, since they cannot be arranged afterwards.

q.q: How does a business continuity plan relate to a disaster recovery plan?
o: It is another name for the IT disaster recovery plan with the same scope
It covers only the IT systems, while disaster recovery covers staff and premises
It replaces the disaster recovery plan once the systems have been restored
It covers the whole organisation, of which IT disaster recovery is one part
q.why: A business continuity plan covers staff, premises and suppliers; IT disaster recovery is one part of it.

q.q: Which is one of the four minimum contents of a disaster recovery plan?
o: The company's marketing strategy
A risk register for the software project
Staff salary details
An alternative site to operate from
q.why: The four contents are critical data, key personnel, backup and recovery processes, and an alternative site.

q.q: In the CCEA textbook, what are recovery point objectives (RPOs)?
o: The time limit for recovering each part of the system
The list of parts of the system that will need to be restored
The maximum amount of data, measured in time, that can be lost
The points at which incremental backups are taken
q.why: In the CCEA meaning, RPOs are the parts to restore and RTOs are the time limits. The 'maximum data loss in time' meaning is the industry definition.

q.q: In the CCEA textbook, what is a recovery time objective?
o: The list of parts of the system that need restoring
The time at which the disaster actually occurred
The time limit for recovering each part of the system
The length of time backups are kept before deletion
q.why: RTO = the time limit for recovery of each part.

q.q: A retailer's plan sets 12 hours to take online orders again and 6 days to run monthly payroll. Why is online ordering given the shorter time?
o: Payroll data is archived, so it cannot be restored sooner
It is a more critical business function, so it gets higher priority
Online orders use incremental backups, which restore fastest
Payroll is not one of the recovery point objectives
q.why: The most critical business functions get the highest priority and the shortest recovery times.

q.q: In industry, what does an RPO of one hour usually mean?
o: Every system must be restored within one hour
The recovery plan must be tested every hour
Backups or replication must happen at least hourly
Staff must be on standby for one hour
q.why: Industry defines RPO as the maximum acceptable data loss in time, so an hour's RPO needs at least hourly backups. Restoring within a time limit is the RTO.

q.q: Which technique helps an organisation meet its RTOs by giving rapid restoration after a local disaster?
o: Private online (cloud) storage
Archiving inactive data each year
Taking only full backups on site
A walk-through test of the plan
q.why: The notes list private cloud storage for rapid restoration, off-site backups, third-party hosting and standby staff.

q.q: In a simulated test of a disaster recovery plan, what happens?
o: Participants step through the plan on paper only
Backups are permanently deleted to test the archive
Working systems are deliberately disabled and actually recovered
No staff take part, so the test is fully automatic
q.why: A simulation actually recovers systems, checking backups restore and time limits are realistic. A walk-through is on paper.

q.q: Which is an advantage of a theoretical (walk-through) test compared with a simulated test?
o: It proves the backups really do restore
It causes little disruption and costs less
It checks the time limits are realistic
It is a far more thorough test overall
q.why: Walk-throughs are low in disruption and cost; simulations are more thorough and check real restores and timings.
